headline: High: haystack’s MCP/networked defaults create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error risk when paired with a content-writing repo that can supply untrusted instructions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Profile A is a content-writing repo with no I/O surfaces, so it is not itself a bridge. Profile B exposes MCP servers and broad network egress, which makes it plausible that A’s generated text could be fed into B through a shared workspace or manual handoff. The pathway is not directly documented, so I choose medium rather than low because B’s default surfaces are instruction-parsing prone.
conditions: IF agent_b ingests agent_a output from a shared workspace or MCP tool result without provenance checks, prompt injection is possible.
IF agent_a content is copied into agent_b prompts as trusted instructions, B can be steered.
mitigations: Disable MCP routes that accept raw text from agent_a.
Add a provenance tag to all agent_a outputs before B reads them.
Require a human review step before B executes instructions from A.
Restrict B to allowlisted prompt templates only.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches no data classes and has no filesystem or network surface, while agent B only lists anonymous usage statistics and broad egress. There is no documented shared workspace or sensitive data class, so leakage is limited to unusual operator setup. Because B can transmit context externally, I keep this at low rather than none.
conditions: IF agent_a is placed in a shared workspace with sensitive files, B could upload them via network egress.
IF operator routes private prompts through B, those prompts may leave the local environment.
mitigations: Keep A and B in separate workspaces.
Do not place sensitive files in any directory B can read.
Disable B network egress for non-public tasks.
Use a redaction step before sending A output to B.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention policies.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has no declared write, network, or concurrency capabilities, so it cannot contend for mutable resources on its own. B has network egress and MCP access, but no filesystem or git write is documented. The pair therefore has only limited overlap, and any conflict would require extra orchestration not shown in either profile.
conditions: IF an orchestrator grants both agents write access to the same mutable resource, conflicts can occur.
IF B is configured with additional write scopes not shown in the profile, contention risk increases.
mitigations: Keep both agents read-only by default.
Separate mutable resources per agent.
Avoid shared git or database writes.
Add a lock around any shared artifact.
requires-engineering: implement optimistic-concurrency checks.

D_cascading_error.rationale: B is a search-RAG agent with MCP and REST access, so it can plausibly act on A’s outputs. A is a content-writing repo, meaning its text may be treated as authoritative by downstream tooling. Without a documented verification step, A’s generated content can cascade into B’s retrieval or action flow in default-style integrations.
conditions: IF B consumes A-generated text as factual input without verification, errors can propagate.
IF B uses A output to populate prompts, citations, or tool calls, downstream actions may be wrong.
mitigations: Insert a verification step before B uses A output.
Require source citations for any factual claim from A.
Limit B to read-only retrieval when fed A content.
Flag low-confidence A outputs for human review.
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking gates.

E_compliance.rationale: No residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for A, and B only touches anonymous usage statistics. The pair does not show PHI, EU PII, or regulated data flow, so compliance risk is limited to generic logging/retention concerns. I cite B only because A has no compliance-relevant data classes or controls listed.
conditions: IF regulated data is introduced into B’s prompts or logs, compliance obligations may change.
IF A is used to generate content containing personal data, retention controls become relevant.
mitigations: Avoid sending regulated data to B.
Review B logging settings before use.
Keep A outputs free of personal data.
Document retention for any shared artifacts.
requires-engineering: add residency and retention policy enforcement.
